_comment: How-do-I recipes. Joe matches a user's query against `triggers` (substring/keyword match) and returns title + code + notes. Languages: python, javascript, typescript, bash, git.

recipes.title: Read a text file in Python
recipes.code:
with open('path/to/file.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    content = f.read()

# Line by line (memory-friendly for big files):
with open('path/to/file.txt') as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.rstrip())
recipes.notes: `'r'` is the default mode. The `with` block auto-closes the file. Pass `encoding='utf-8'` for non-ASCII text. For binary, use `'rb'`.

recipes.title: Write a text file in Python
recipes.code:
with open('out.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('hello
')
    f.writelines(['line1
', 'line2
'])
recipes.notes: `'w'` truncates the file. Use `'a'` to append. `writelines` does NOT add newlines for you.

recipes.title: Append to a file in Python
recipes.code:
with open('log.txt', 'a', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('new line\n')
recipes.notes: `'a'` creates the file if missing. Each program run keeps appending — rotate logs if you care about size.

recipes.title: Read a binary file in Python
recipes.code:
with open('image.png', 'rb') as f:
    data = f.read()  # bytes object
recipes.notes: Use `'rb'`/`'wb'` for non-text files (images, archives, executables). Don't pass `encoding` with binary modes.

recipes.title: Read a JSON file in Python
recipes.code:
import json

with open('data.json') as f:
    data = json.load(f)

# From a string:
obj = json.loads('{"a": 1}')
recipes.notes: `json.load` reads from a file, `json.loads` from a string. Raises `json.JSONDecodeError` on bad JSON.

recipes.title: Write JSON (pretty) in Python
recipes.code:
import json

with open('out.json', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
recipes.notes: `indent=2` for pretty output. `ensure_ascii=False` keeps unicode readable. Use `default=str` to serialize datetimes.

recipes.title: Read a CSV with the csv module
recipes.code:
import csv

with open('data.csv', newline='') as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row['name'], row['age'])
recipes.notes: `DictReader` uses the first row as headers. Always pass `newline=''` on the open() — avoids weird line splits on Windows.

recipes.title: Write a CSV in Python
recipes.code:
import csv

rows = [{'name': 'Ada', 'age': 36}, {'name': 'Joe', 'age': 9}]
with open('out.csv', 'w', newline='') as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=['name', 'age'])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(rows)
recipes.notes: `newline=''` prevents blank lines between rows. For huge data, use `csv.writer` with row tuples — slightly faster.

print(df.head())
print(df.dtypes)

recipes.title: HTTP GET with requests
recipes.code:
import requests

r = requests.get('https://api.example.com/users', params={'q': 'joe'}, timeout=10)
r.raise_for_status()
data = r.json()
recipes.notes: Always set a `timeout` — default is no timeout, which can hang forever. `raise_for_status()` throws on 4xx/5xx.

recipes.title: HTTP POST with requests
recipes.code:
import requests

r = requests.post(
    'https://api.example.com/items',
    json={'name': 'banana'},
    headers={'Authorization': 'Bearer TOKEN'},
    timeout=10,
)
r.raise_for_status()
print(r.json())
recipes.notes: Use `json=` to send JSON (sets Content-Type automatically). Use `data=` for form-encoded, `files=` for uploads.

recipes.title: HTTP GET with urllib (stdlib)
recipes.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen, Request
import json

req = Request('https://httpbin.org/get', headers={'User-Agent': 'monkey-joe/1.0'})
with urlopen(req, timeout=10) as resp:
    data = json.loads(resp.read())

recipes.title: Async HTTP with httpx
recipes.code:
import httpx, asyncio

async def fetch():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        r = await client.get('https://api.example.com/')
        return r.json()

asyncio.run(fetch())
recipes.notes: httpx has the same API as requests but supports async, HTTP/2, and connection pooling. Reuse the `AsyncClient` across requests.

recipes.title: Async HTTP with aiohttp
recipes.code:
import aiohttp, asyncio

async def fetch(url):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(url, timeout=10) as r:
            return await r.json()

asyncio.run(fetch('https://api.example.com/'))
recipes.notes: For lots of concurrent requests, use `asyncio.gather` with a shared session. Don't create a new session per request.

recipes.title: Run a subprocess and capture output
recipes.code:
import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(
    ['ls', '-la'],
    capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
)
print(result.stdout)
recipes.notes: `check=True` raises on non-zero exit. `text=True` decodes bytes to str. Pass a list (not a string) unless you need `shell=True`.

recipes.title: Pipe between subprocesses (Python)
recipes.code:
import subprocess

ps = subprocess.Popen(['ps', 'aux'], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
grep = subprocess.run(['grep', 'python'], stdin=ps.stdout, capture_output=True, text=True)
ps.stdout.close()
print(grep.stdout)
recipes.notes: Close the upstream stdout after handoff so SIGPIPE works correctly. Simpler alternative: `subprocess.run('ps aux | grep python', shell=True)` (watch for injection).

recipes.title: Run a subprocess in the background
recipes.code:
import subprocess

proc = subprocess.Popen(['long-running', 'job'])
# ... do other work ...
proc.terminate()  # or proc.wait() to block
recipes.notes: `Popen` returns immediately. Use `proc.poll()` to check if done. `terminate()` sends SIGTERM, `kill()` SIGKILL.

recipes.title: argparse basics
recipes.code:
import argparse

p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Greet someone.')
p.add_argument('name')
p.add_argument('--shout', action='store_true')
p.add_argument('--count', type=int, default=1)
args = p.parse_args()

msg = f'Hello, {args.name}!'
print((msg.upper() if args.shout else msg) * args.count)
recipes.notes: Positional args have no `--`. `action='store_true'` for booleans. `type=int` auto-validates.

recipes.title: argparse subcommands
recipes.code:
import argparse

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
sub = p.add_subparsers(dest='cmd', required=True)

add = sub.add_parser('add')
add.add_argument('item')

ls = sub.add_parser('list')

args = p.parse_args()
if args.cmd == 'add':
    print('adding', args.item)
elif args.cmd == 'list':
    print('listing')
recipes.notes: `required=True` makes the subcommand mandatory. Each subparser is its own ArgumentParser with its own args.

port = int(os.getenv('DB_PORT', '5432'))

recipes.title: f-string formatting
recipes.code:
name, count = 'Joe', 3
print(f'Hello {name}, you have {count} items.')
print(f'{3.14159:.2f}')        # 3.14
print(f'{42:08d}')             # 00000042
print(f'{count=}')             # count=3 (debug)
print(f'{name!r}')             # 'Joe' (repr)
recipes.notes: Use `{var=}` (Py 3.8+) for quick debugging. `:.2f` = 2 decimal places. `!r` = repr, `!s` = str.

recipes.title: Current date/time in Python
recipes.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone

now = datetime.now()                        # local naive
utc = datetime.now(timezone.utc)            # aware UTC
print(now.isoformat())
print(utc.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'))
recipes.notes: Prefer timezone-aware datetimes (`timezone.utc` or `zoneinfo.ZoneInfo`). Naive datetimes cause bugs at DST boundaries.

recipes.title: Parse a date string
recipes.code:
from datetime import datetime

d = datetime.strptime('2026-05-14', '%Y-%m-%d')
d2 = datetime.fromisoformat('2026-05-14T10:30:00')
recipes.notes: `fromisoformat` is fastest if your input is ISO-8601. For fuzzy formats, use `dateutil.parser.parse` (pip install python-dateutil).

recipes.title: Add days/hours to a date
recipes.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

now = datetime.now()
tomorrow = now + timedelta(days=1)
in_3h = now + timedelta(hours=3)
delta = tomorrow - now  # timedelta(days=1)
print(delta.total_seconds())
recipes.notes: `timedelta` supports days, seconds, microseconds, minutes, hours, weeks. No `months`/`years` — use `dateutil.relativedelta` for those.

recipes.title: Sort a list in Python
recipes.code:
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
asc = sorted(nums)            # new list
desc = sorted(nums, reverse=True)
nums.sort()                    # in place
recipes.notes: `sorted()` returns a new list; `.sort()` mutates. Both are stable (equal items keep order).

recipes.title: Sort by a custom key
recipes.code:
users = [{'name': 'Joe', 'age': 9}, {'name': 'Ada', 'age': 36}]
by_age = sorted(users, key=lambda u: u['age'])
by_name = sorted(users, key=lambda u: u['name'].lower())

# Sort dict by value:
d = {'a': 3, 'b': 1, 'c': 2}
ordered = dict(sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]))
recipes.notes: For multi-key sort: `key=lambda u: (u['age'], u['name'])`. `operator.itemgetter('age')` is faster than a lambda.

recipes.title: Deduplicate a list (preserve order)
recipes.code:
items = ['a', 'b', 'a', 'c', 'b']
unique = list(dict.fromkeys(items))   # ['a', 'b', 'c']

# If order doesn't matter:
unique_unordered = list(set(items))
recipes.notes: `dict.fromkeys` preserves first-seen order (Py 3.7+). `set()` is faster but loses order.

recipes.title: Flatten a nested list
recipes.notes: `chain.from_iterable` only flattens one level. For arbitrary nesting, write a recursive generator.

recipes.title: Group items by a key
recipes.code:
from collections import defaultdict

items = [('fruit', 'apple'), ('veg', 'carrot'), ('fruit', 'pear')]
groups = defaultdict(list)
for cat, name in items:
    groups[cat].append(name)

# itertools.groupby — requires sorted input:
from itertools import groupby
for key, grp in groupby(sorted(items), key=lambda x: x[0]):
    print(key, list(grp))
recipes.notes: `defaultdict` is usually easier and doesn't require sorting. `itertools.groupby` only groups CONSECUTIVE matches.

recipes.title: Chunk a list into N-sized pieces
recipes.notes: Py 3.12+: `itertools.batched(lst, n)` is built in. For iterators (not lists), write a generator that uses `islice`.

recipes.title: Find max/min by key
recipes.code:
users = [{'name': 'Joe', 'age': 9}, {'name': 'Ada', 'age': 36}]
oldest = max(users, key=lambda u: u['age'])
youngest = min(users, key=lambda u: u['age'])
recipes.notes: Pass `default=None` to handle empty iterables without exceptions: `max(xs, key=..., default=None)`.

recipes.title: Count items / most common
recipes.code:
from collections import Counter

words = 'the quick brown fox the lazy dog the'.split()
c = Counter(words)
print(c.most_common(2))  # [('the', 3), ('quick', 1)]
print(c['the'])           # 3
print(c['missing'])       # 0 (no KeyError)
recipes.notes: Counter is a dict subclass. Supports arithmetic: `c1 + c2`, `c1 - c2`, `c1 & c2` (min), `c1 | c2` (max).

recipes.title: Connect to PostgreSQL (psycopg)
recipes.code:
import psycopg  # psycopg3, or psycopg2

with psycopg.connect('postgresql://user:pw@localhost/db') as conn:
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute('SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE active = %s', (True,))
        for row in cur.fetchall():
            print(row)
recipes.notes: Always parameterize queries (`%s` placeholders) — never string-format SQL. psycopg3 supports async; psycopg2 is the older sync-only version.

recipes.title: Connect to SQLite

    conn.execute('INSERT INTO notes(text) VALUES (?)', ('hello',))
    for row in conn.execute('SELECT * FROM notes'):

recipes.title: Connect to MySQL

conn = pymysql.connect(host='localhost', user='root', password='pw', database='app')
try:
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute('SELECT id FROM users WHERE active=%s', (1,))
        print(cur.fetchall())
finally:
    conn.close()
recipes.notes: Alternatives: `mysql-connector-python` (Oracle's official), `aiomysql` for async. Parameterize with `%s` not f-strings.

recipes.title: SQLAlchemy ORM basics
recipes.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, String
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'users'
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50))

engine = create_engine('sqlite:///app.db')
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)

with Session(engine) as s:
    s.add(User(name='Joe'))
    s.commit()
recipes.notes: This is SQLAlchemy 2.x style. For 1.x you used `declarative_base()` and `Column(...)`. Always commit or use `with s.begin()`.

recipes.code:
import asyncio

async def main():
    print('hi')
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    print('bye')

asyncio.run(main())

recipes.title: Run async tasks in parallel (gather)
recipes.code:
import asyncio

async def task(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return n * 2

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(task(1), task(2), task(3))
    print(results)  # [2, 4, 6]

asyncio.run(main())
recipes.notes: `gather` runs concurrently and returns results in order. Use `return_exceptions=True` to keep going if one fails.

recipes.title: Type hints basics
recipes.notes: Hints don't enforce at runtime — they're for tools (mypy, IDEs). Use `from __future__ import annotations` to defer all evaluation.

recipes.title: TypedDict and Protocol
recipes.notes: TypedDict = shape of a dict. Protocol = structural (duck) typing — any class with matching methods passes.

recipes.title: Dataclass example
recipes.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    age: int = 0
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

u = User('Joe', 9)
print(u)  # User(name='Joe', age=9, tags=[])
recipes.notes: Auto-generates `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`. Use `field(default_factory=list)` for mutable defaults — never `tags: list = []`.

recipes.title: Pydantic model
recipes.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1)
    age: int = Field(ge=0)

recipes.title: Enum in Python
recipes.code:
from enum import Enum, auto

class Status(Enum):
    PENDING = auto()
    ACTIVE = auto()
    DONE = auto()

print(Status.ACTIVE.name, Status.ACTIVE.value)
for s in Status:
    print(s)
recipes.notes: Use `StrEnum` (Py 3.11+) when you want string semantics: `class Color(StrEnum): RED='red'`. Members are singletons and hashable.

recipes.title: Generator (yield)
recipes.notes: Generators are lazy — values produced on demand, memory-efficient for large sequences. Use `yield from sub()` to delegate.

recipes.title: Decorator (with and without args)
recipes.notes: Always use `@wraps(fn)` so the decorated function keeps its name/docstring. Decorators with args add one more layer.

recipes.title: Custom context manager
recipes.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager
import time

@contextmanager
def timer(label):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        print(f'{label}: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s')

with timer('work'):
    sum(range(10_000_000))
recipes.notes: The `finally` block is critical — it runs even if the `with` body raises. For classes, implement `__enter__` / `__exit__`.

recipes.title: Regex basics (re module)
recipes.code:
import re

text = 'Email me at joe@example.com or ada@example.org'

m = re.search(r'\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b', text)
if m:
    print(m.group())  # joe@example.com

all_emails = re.findall(r'\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b', text)
fixed = re.sub(r'@', ' [at] ', text)

# Match at start vs anywhere:
re.match(r'\d+', '42abc')   # matches
re.match(r'\d+', 'abc42')   # None
re.search(r'\d+', 'abc42')  # matches
recipes.notes: Always use raw strings (`r'...'`) for regex. `match` anchors to start; `search` finds anywhere. `findall` returns list of matches.

recipes.title: Walrus operator (:=)
recipes.notes: Py 3.8+. Useful for combining a check with capturing the value. Don't overuse — can hurt readability.

recipes.title: pytest fixture
recipes.notes: Code before `yield` is setup, after is teardown. Use `scope='session'` to share a fixture across the whole test run.

recipes.title: pytest parametrize

recipes.title: Mock a function
recipes.code:
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock

# Patch where it's USED, not where it's defined:
with patch('mymodule.requests.get') as mock_get:
    mock_get.return_value.json.return_value = {'ok': True}
    result = mymodule.fetch()
    mock_get.assert_called_once()
recipes.notes: Common gotcha: patch the import path where the function is LOOKED UP, not where it's defined. `pytest-mock` provides a `mocker` fixture for nicer syntax.

recipes.title: @property decorator
recipes.notes: Use properties to add validation or computed values without changing the public API. Don't make every attribute a property — only when you need logic.

recipes.title: Class inheritance
recipes.notes: Always call `super().__init__()` to run parent setup. Override methods by redefining them in the child.

recipes.title: Abstract base class
recipes.notes: ABCs enforce that subclasses implement required methods. Use Protocols instead if you want structural typing without inheritance.

recipes.title: Singleton pattern
recipes.notes: Modules are already singletons in Python — usually a plain module with module-level values is simpler than a Singleton class.

recipes.title: Memoize with lru_cache
recipes.notes: Args must be hashable (no lists/dicts). Py 3.9+: `@cache` is `lru_cache(maxsize=None)`. Clear with `fib.cache_clear()`.

recipes.title: ThreadPoolExecutor
recipes.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
import requests

urls = ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com', 'https://c.com']

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as ex:
    futures = {ex.submit(requests.get, u): u for u in urls}
    for f in as_completed(futures):
        print(futures[f], f.result().status_code)
recipes.notes: Threads are great for I/O-bound work (HTTP, file I/O). For CPU-bound work, use `ProcessPoolExecutor` instead — GIL blocks real parallelism on threads.

recipes.title: Hash a string or file (sha256)

recipes.title: Catch specific exceptions

recipes.title: Re-raise with context

recipes.title: Custom exception class

recipes.title: try/except/else/finally

recipes.title: Path operations in Node

recipes.title: fetch POST with JSON

recipes.title: axios POST with headers

recipes.title: Multipart form upload (Node 20+)

recipes.title: Run a shell command in Node

recipes.title: Environment variables in Node
recipes.notes: `process.env` values are always strings. Use `??` (nullish coalescing) for defaults. Cast numbers/bools yourself.

recipes.title: Load .env in Node
recipes.notes: Node 20.6+ has `--env-file=.env` built-in — no library needed. dotenv won't overwrite existing env vars unless you pass `{ override: true }`.

recipes.title: CLI args with yargs

recipes.title: Date basics in JavaScript
recipes.notes: Built-in Date is rough. Reach for `date-fns` (tree-shakeable) or `dayjs` (small, immutable) for anything beyond basics.

recipes.title: Format a date (date-fns / Intl)

recipes.title: Array map / filter / reduce
recipes.notes: Always pass the initial value to `reduce` (the `0` above) — without it, the first element becomes the accumulator and weird things happen with empty arrays.

recipes.title: Flatten an array
recipes.notes: `flat(Infinity)` for arbitrary nesting. `flatMap` = map + flat(1) — handy for splitting strings or expanding arrays.

recipes.title: Sort an array of objects
recipes.notes: `sort` mutates! Spread to a new array first if you want immutability. `localeCompare` handles unicode/accents correctly.

recipes.title: Deduplicate an array
recipes.notes: `Set` works on primitives. For objects, dedupe by a key (id, email) using a Map or `Object.fromEntries`.

recipes.title: Sum an array
recipes.notes: The `0` initial value matters — without it, `[].reduce((a,b) => a+b)` throws.

recipes.title: Group array by key
recipes.notes: `Object.groupBy` is new — check support. The reduce version works everywhere. `??=` only assigns if currently nullish.

recipes.title: Object: keys, values, entries
recipes.notes: Order is insertion order for string keys (integer-like keys come first numerically). For arbitrary key types use a `Map`.

recipes.title: Object spread / merge
recipes.notes: Later spreads override earlier ones. This is SHALLOW — nested objects are still shared references. Use `structuredClone` for deep copies.

recipes.title: Deep clone an object
recipes.code: const clone = structuredClone(original);
recipes.notes: Built into modern Node + browsers. Handles Maps, Sets, Dates, typed arrays. Won't clone functions or DOM nodes.

recipes.title: Destructuring with defaults
recipes.notes: The `= {}` after a nested destructure is critical when the parent might be undefined — without it you'll get a TypeError.

recipes.title: Promise.all / allSettled
recipes.notes: Use `allSettled` when you want every result, success or fail. `all` is faster when you can short-circuit on error.

recipes.title: async/await pattern
recipes.notes: `await` only works inside `async` (or at top level of ES modules). Always wrap awaits in try/catch or attach `.catch` somewhere.

recipes.title: Sleep / setTimeout as promise
recipes.notes: Node 16+ has `import { setTimeout } from 'node:timers/promises'` — `await setTimeout(1000)` natively.

recipes.title: Debounce a function
recipes.notes: Debounce = wait for quiet. Throttle = fire at most once per N ms. Use debounce for search input, throttle for scroll handlers.

recipes.title: Node EventEmitter
recipes.notes: EventEmitter is synchronous — listeners run in order. Default max listeners is 10; bump with `bus.setMaxListeners(20)` for high-fanout buses.

recipes.title: Stream a file
recipes.notes: `pipeline` handles errors and cleanup correctly across all streams. Don't use `.pipe()` directly — error handling is messy.

recipes.title: Server-Sent Events (Express)
recipes.notes: SSE is one-way (server → client) and simpler than WebSockets. Each event ends with two newlines. Client side: `new EventSource('/events')`.

recipes.title: WebSocket server (ws)
recipes.notes: Messages arrive as Buffers — call `.toString()` for text. Use a heartbeat (ping/pong) for long-lived connections.

recipes.title: Express GET / POST
recipes.notes: `express.json()` is required to parse JSON request bodies. Use `express.urlencoded({ extended: true })` for form posts.

recipes.title: Express middleware
recipes.notes: Middleware takes `(req, res, next)` — call `next()` to continue, or send a response to short-circuit. Error middleware has 4 args.

recipes.title: Express error handling
recipes.notes: Async route errors don't propagate automatically in old Express — wrap in try/catch and call `next(err)`. Express 5 fixes this.

recipes.title: Fastify basics
recipes.notes: Faster than Express, schema-first (JSON schema validation built in). Handlers return the body — Fastify serializes automatically.

recipes.title: Connect to PostgreSQL (pg)
recipes.notes: Always use the pool (not a single client). Parameterize with `$1`/`$2` — never template strings. Close with `await pool.end()` on shutdown.

recipes.title: MongoDB with mongoose
recipes.notes: Mongoose adds schemas/validation on top of MongoDB. For raw driver use `mongodb` package. Always `await` queries — they return Promises.

recipes.title: Connect to Redis (ioredis)
recipes.notes: `'EX', 60` = expire in 60 seconds. ioredis supports cluster, sentinel, pub/sub out of the box. Alternative: `redis` (official).

recipes.title: Prisma ORM basics

recipes.title: Send email with nodemailer
recipes.notes: Use app-passwords for Gmail. For transactional email at scale, use a service like Postmark/Resend with their SDK.

recipes.title: Hash a password (bcrypt)
recipes.notes: Cost factor 10-12 is current standard. Higher = slower = more secure. Never store plain passwords. Alternatives: argon2 (modern), scrypt (stdlib).

recipes.title: JWT sign / verify
recipes.notes: Use a strong, long secret (32+ random bytes). Prefer HS256 for symmetric, RS256 if you need separate signing/verifying keys.

recipes.title: CORS in Express
recipes.notes: `credentials: true` allows cookies — required for session-based auth. Don't use `origin: '*'` with credentials (browsers refuse it).

recipes.title: Rate limiting (express-rate-limit)
recipes.notes: In-memory by default — won't share across processes. For multi-instance, back it with Redis via `rate-limit-redis`.

recipes.title: Structured logging with pino
recipes.notes: Pino is the fastest JSON logger for Node — production friendly. Winston is more featureful but slower. For dev pretty-print, use `pino-pretty`.

recipes.title: Read a JSON file in Node

const data = JSON.parse(await readFile('data.json', 'utf8'));

await writeFile('out.json', JSON.stringify(data, null, 2));

recipes.title: Parse CSV with csv-parse
recipes.notes: Use the async version (`csv-parse`) for big files. `columns: true` makes each row an object with header keys.

recipes.title: Generate UUID (crypto.randomUUID)
recipes.notes: Built into Node 14.17+ and modern browsers — no `uuid` package needed. Always v4 (random).

recipes.title: Random numbers and picks
recipes.notes: `Math.random` is NOT cryptographically secure. Use `crypto.randomInt` / `randomBytes` for tokens, keys, anything security-sensitive.

recipes.title: ES Modules vs CommonJS
recipes.notes: ESM is the future — supports tree-shaking, top-level await. Use `.cjs` / `.mjs` extensions if you need to mix. ESM imports need the `.js` extension in Node.

recipes.title: Top-level await
recipes.notes: Only works in ES modules. Doesn't work in CommonJS or in non-module browser scripts.

recipes.title: Dynamic import
recipes.notes: Returns a Promise. Works in both ESM and CommonJS. Useful for code splitting in bundlers and conditional loading.

recipes.title: Run TypeScript with tsx

recipes.notes: `tsx` is faster than `ts-node` and supports ESM out of the box. Node 22+ has experimental built-in TS via `node --experimental-strip-types`.

recipes.title: Worker threads
recipes.notes: Use for CPU-heavy work. For I/O, async is enough. Each worker has its own V8 instance — communication via messages (structured-cloned).

recipes.title: Cluster mode (fork workers)
recipes.notes: Each worker is a full Node process — uses all CPU cores for a single port. Modern alternative: PM2 or running multiple containers behind a load balancer.

recipes.title: Jest test basics
recipes.notes: `toBe` = strict equality (===). Use `toEqual` for deep object comparison. ESM with Jest needs the `--experimental-vm-modules` flag.

recipes.title: Jest mocks
recipes.notes: `jest.mock` is hoisted to the top of the file. `mockResolvedValue` for promises, `mockReturnValue` for sync. `jest.fn()` for ad-hoc mocks.

recipes.title: Vitest test basics
recipes.notes: Vitest has the same API as Jest but works natively with Vite/ESM/TypeScript — usually no config needed. Run with `npx vitest`.

recipes.title: Snapshot test
recipes.notes: Snapshots are committed to git. Review diffs carefully on changes — easy to update past mistakes. Don't snapshot huge things.

recipes.title: Format with prettier

# Check (CI):

recipes.notes: Pair with ESLint via `eslint-config-prettier` (turns off conflicting rules). Add a pre-commit hook with `lint-staged` + `husky`.

recipes.title: ESLint setup
recipes.notes: ESLint 9+ uses flat config (eslint.config.js). For TypeScript: `typescript-eslint`. For React: `eslint-plugin-react`.

recipes.title: Type alias vs interface
recipes.notes: Interfaces can be re-opened (declaration merging) — useful for extending lib types. Otherwise prefer `type` for unions, mapped types, function signatures.

recipes.title: Generic function
recipes.notes: TypeScript usually infers generics from arguments. Add constraints with `<T extends Foo>` to require a shape.

recipes.title: Generic class
recipes.notes: Generic param is part of the class type — `Stack<number>` and `Stack<string>` are different types.

recipes.title: Utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, Readonly)
recipes.code:
type User = { id: number; name: string; email: string };

type UserUpdate = Partial<User>;             // all optional
type UserKey = Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>;    // subset
type UserNoId = Omit<User, 'id'>;            // exclude
type UserMap = Record<string, User>;         // dict-like
type Frozen = Readonly<User>;                // all readonly
type RequiredUser = Required<User>;          // all required
recipes.notes: These cover 90% of object-type manipulation. `Required` is the inverse of `Partial`. `Record<K, V>` is shorthand for `{ [k in K]: V }`.

recipes.title: Type guards
recipes.notes: `x is string` is a *type predicate* — tells TS the function narrows the type. TS narrows automatically on `typeof`, `instanceof`, equality checks.

recipes.title: Discriminated union
recipes.notes: The `kind` field (any literal property) is the discriminator. TS narrows inside each `case`. Add `default: const _: never = s;` for exhaustiveness.

recipes.title: Mapped type
recipes.notes: `keyof T` gives the union of T's keys. Modifiers: `readonly`, `?`. Use `+`/`-` to add/remove: `-readonly`, `-?`.

recipes.title: Conditional type
recipes.notes: `infer U` captures a type for use in the true branch. Conditional types distribute over unions: `ToArr<string | number> = string[] | number[]`.

recipes.title: Template literal types
recipes.notes: Built-in helpers: `Uppercase<S>`, `Lowercase<S>`, `Capitalize<S>`, `Uncapitalize<S>`. Powerful for API/event-name typing.

recipes.title: Enum vs const assertion
recipes.notes: Plain enums generate runtime code and have weird bidirectional mapping for numeric. The `as const` pattern is more TS-idiomatic, tree-shakeable, and JSON-safe.

recipes.title: Module declarations / augmentation
recipes.notes: Use this when a library has no types or you want to add fields. The augmentation must be in a file TS sees (referenced via tsconfig).

recipes.title: Ambient types (.d.ts)
recipes.notes: The `export {}` is critical when using `declare global` — without it, the file is a script and `declare global` is unnecessary. Reference the file in tsconfig.json `include`.

recipes.title: React functional component typing
recipes.notes: Prefer typing props directly rather than `React.FC` — `FC` adds an implicit `children` and isn't generic-friendly. For children, add `children: React.ReactNode`.

recipes.title: useState typing
recipes.notes: Explicit type when the initial value doesn't capture the full shape (null, empty array, etc.). For complex state, `useReducer` is clearer.

recipes.title: useEffect with cleanup
recipes.notes: Always return a cleanup if you set up subscriptions/timers/fetches. AbortController is the modern way to cancel an in-flight fetch.

recipes.title: React event types
recipes.notes: Generic event types take the element type. For mixed elements use a broader type like `HTMLElement`. Inline handlers usually don't need types — TS infers.

recipes.title: React useRef typing
recipes.notes: Initial value `null` and the type `<HTMLInputElement>` are the typical pattern for DOM refs. Use `useRef<T>(undefined as T)` if you want a mutable ref without null checks.

recipes.title: Async function return type
recipes.notes: Always declare the resolved type as `Promise<T>`. TS infers, but explicit is better for public APIs.

recipes.title: satisfies vs as
recipes.notes: Prefer `satisfies` to `as` — `as` is a forced cast that can hide bugs. `satisfies` checks the value matches the type without widening it.

recipes.title: Index signature
recipes.notes: Once you add an index signature, ALL declared properties must be assignable to it. `Record<K, V>` is usually cleaner.

recipes.title: Tuple types
recipes.notes: Tuples are fixed-length, position-typed arrays. Useful for React-style return values: `[state, setState]`.

recipes.title: ReadonlyArray
recipes.notes: Use `readonly T[]` for function params you won't mutate — lets callers pass immutable arrays too. `ReadonlyArray<T>` is the long form.

recipes.title: Function overloads
recipes.notes: Overload signatures (the lines without bodies) define the call signatures. The implementation must be compatible with all of them. Often a single union signature is cleaner.

recipes.title: never vs unknown vs any
recipes.notes: `unknown` is the type-safe `any` — forces narrowing. `never` is useful in unreachable branches and exhaustive switches: `const _: never = x;`.

recipes.title: Promise<T> and Awaited<T>
recipes.notes: `Awaited<T>` unwraps any nested promises (`Promise<Promise<X>>` → `X`). `ReturnType<typeof fn>` extracts return type of a function value.

recipes.title: if / elif / else
recipes.code:
if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then
  echo 'exists'
elif [[ -d "$file" ]]; then
  echo 'is a directory'
else
  echo 'missing'
fi
recipes.notes: Use `[[ ... ]]` (bash) not `[ ... ]` (POSIX) — fewer quoting gotchas. Common tests: `-f` file, `-d` dir, `-z` empty string, `-n` non-empty, `=` equal, `-eq` numeric.

recipes.title: for loops (range, files, array)
recipes.code:
# C-style range:
for ((i = 0; i < 5; i++)); do echo $i; done

# Sequence:
for i in {1..5}; do echo $i; done

# Files matching a glob:
for f in *.txt; do echo "$f"; done

# Array:
arr=(one two three)
for x in "${arr[@]}"; do echo "$x"; done
recipes.notes: Always quote `"${arr[@]}"` to preserve elements with spaces. `{1..5}` is brace expansion — happens before variable expansion.

triggers: read file line by line bash
recipes.title: Read a file line by line
recipes.code:
while IFS= read -r line; do
  echo "got: $line"
done < input.txt
recipes.notes: `IFS=` prevents stripping leading/trailing whitespace. `-r` disables backslash escapes. This is the safe canonical form.

recipes.title: Read user input
recipes.code:
read -p 'Name: ' name
echo "hello $name"

# Silent (passwords):
read -s -p 'Password: ' pw
echo
recipes.notes: `-s` hides the input. `-t 10` adds a 10-second timeout. `-r` is good practice to disable backslash processing.

recipes.title: Functions and arguments
recipes.code:
greet() {
  local name="$1"
  local count="${2:-1}"   # default 1
  for ((i = 0; i < count; i++)); do
    echo "hello $name"
  done
}

greet 'joe' 3
recipes.notes: `$1` `$2` are positional args. `$@` = all args (each quoted), `$*` = all args (one string). Always use `local` for function vars.

recipes.title: Default values for variables
recipes.code:
name="${1:-anon}"               # default if unset OR empty
name="${NAME:?must be set}"      # error out if unset
: "${PORT:=3000}"                # assign default if unset
recipes.notes: `:-` use default. `:=` assign default. `:?` error message. `:+` use alternate (if set, use this — else empty).

recipes.title: Check if a variable is set
recipes.code:
if [[ -z "${VAR-}" ]]; then
  echo 'VAR is unset or empty'
fi

# Distinguish unset from empty:
if [[ -z "${VAR+x}" ]]; then echo 'unset'; fi
recipes.notes: `${VAR-}` returns empty if unset (avoids errors with `set -u`). `${VAR+x}` returns 'x' only if set — useful to tell unset vs empty.

recipes.title: Arithmetic in bash
recipes.code:
i=5
((i++))            # increment
result=$((i * 2))   # 12
if (( i > 3 )); then echo big; fi

# Floats need bc or awk:
echo 'scale=2; 10 / 3' | bc
recipes.notes: `(( ))` is integer-only. For floats use `bc -l`, `awk`, or just call Python. No `$` needed inside `(( ))`.

recipes.title: String length, substring, replace
recipes.code:
s='hello world'
echo "${#s}"            # 11 (length)
echo "${s:0:5}"         # 'hello' (substring)
echo "${s/world/joe}"   # replace first
echo "${s//l/L}"        # replace all
echo "${s%world}"       # remove shortest match from end
echo "${s#hello}"       # remove shortest match from start
echo "${s^^}"           # uppercase
recipes.notes: These are all parameter expansion — no external programs needed. `^^` upper, `,,` lower (bash 4+).

recipes.title: Arrays in bash
recipes.code:
arr=(one two three)
arr+=('four')
echo "${arr[0]}"            # one
echo "${arr[@]}"            # all elements
echo "${#arr[@]}"           # length

for x in "${arr[@]}"; do echo "$x"; done
recipes.notes: Always quote `"${arr[@]}"` — without quotes, spaces in elements get split. Bash arrays are zero-indexed.

recipes.title: Associative array (hash)
recipes.code:
declare -A user
user[name]='Joe'
user[age]=9

echo "${user[name]}"
for k in "${!user[@]}"; do
  echo "$k = ${user[$k]}"
done
recipes.notes: Bash 4+ only. macOS ships bash 3 — use `brew install bash` or zsh. `${!user[@]}` gives keys, `${user[@]}` gives values.

recipes.title: Read from stdin
recipes.code:
while IFS= read -r line; do
  echo "line: $line"
done

# Usage:
# cat file.txt | ./script.sh
# echo 'hi' | ./script.sh
recipes.notes: Same pattern as reading from a file, but no `< file` redirection. Use `[[ -t 0 ]]` to detect if stdin is a terminal vs pipe.

recipes.title: Capture command output
recipes.code:
files=$(ls -1)
date=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
result="$(curl -s https://example.com)"

# Multi-line:
output=$(cat <<-EOF
  line 1
  line 2
EOF
)
recipes.notes: Use `$(...)` not backticks — they nest cleanly and are easier to read. Always quote `"$(...)"` if the output may have spaces.

recipes.title: Capture stderr / redirect
recipes.code:
# stderr -> stdout (combine):
cmd 2>&1

# Separate streams:
cmd > out.log 2> err.log

# Discard stderr:
cmd 2> /dev/null

# Capture both in a variable:
output=$(cmd 2>&1)
recipes.notes: Order matters: `> file 2>&1` works, `2>&1 > file` does NOT (redirects stderr to old stdout, then redirects stdout to file).

recipes.title: Silence output
recipes.code:
cmd > /dev/null            # discard stdout
cmd 2> /dev/null           # discard stderr
cmd > /dev/null 2>&1       # discard both
cmd &> /dev/null            # bash shortcut for both
recipes.notes: `&>` is bash-specific — POSIX shells need `> file 2>&1`. Use for commands where you only care about exit code.

recipes.title: Tee output to file AND stdout
recipes.code:
cmd | tee output.log

# Append instead of overwrite:
cmd | tee -a output.log

# With sudo, useful pattern:
echo 'line' | sudo tee -a /etc/somefile
recipes.notes: `tee` is also the trick for writing to root-owned files with `sudo` — the redirection `> file` doesn't get sudo, but `sudo tee` does.

recipes.title: Run in background and wait
recipes.code:
task1 &
task2 &
task3 &
wait                  # wait for all
echo 'all done'

# Capture PIDs:
task1 & pid1=$!
wait "$pid1"
echo "exit: $?"
recipes.notes: `$!` = PID of the last backgrounded job. `wait` with no args waits for all jobs. `wait $pid` waits for one and gives you its exit code in `$?`.

recipes.title: Trap signals for cleanup
recipes.code:
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT
trap 'echo interrupted; exit 130' INT

# do stuff with $tmpdir...
recipes.notes: `EXIT` runs on any exit (success, failure, signal). `INT` is Ctrl+C. Combine: `trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM`.

recipes.title: Strict mode
recipes.notes: `-e` exit on error, `-u` error on unset var, `-o pipefail` make pipes fail loudly. `IFS=$'\n\t'` makes word splitting more predictable. Add at the top of every script.

recipes.title: Exit codes
recipes.code:
cmd
echo "exit: $?"

if cmd; then echo ok; else echo "failed ($?)"; fi

# Return from function:
my_func() {
  [[ -f "$1" ]] || return 1
  return 0
}
recipes.notes: 0 = success, 1-255 = error. Conventions: 1 general, 2 misuse, 126 not executable, 127 not found, 128+N killed by signal N.

recipes.title: find: name, mtime, size, exec
recipes.code:
find . -name '*.log'
find . -iname '*.JPG' -type f
find . -mtime -7        # modified last 7 days
find . -size +100M      # bigger than 100MB
find . -name '*.tmp' -delete
find . -name '*.txt' -exec wc -l {} +
recipes.notes: `-iname` is case-insensitive. `-mtime -7` last 7 days, `+7` older than 7 days. `-exec ... {} +` batches args (faster than `\;`).

recipes.title: find + xargs
recipes.code:
find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 rm
find . -name '*.txt' -print0 | xargs -0 -n1 -P4 process_file
recipes.notes: Always use `-print0` / `-0` for filenames with spaces or newlines. `-P4` runs 4 in parallel. `-n1` = one arg per invocation.

recipes.title: sed: substitute, in-place
recipes.code:
sed 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt              # print with replacement
sed -i 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt            # GNU in-place
sed -i '' 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt         # macOS/BSD in-place
sed -n '5,10p' file.txt                  # print lines 5-10
sed '/^#/d' file.txt                     # delete comment lines
recipes.notes: `-i ''` is required on macOS (BSD sed). For portability, write to a temp file and `mv`. `/g` = replace all on a line.

recipes.title: awk: print fields, sum a column
recipes.code:
awk '{print $1, $3}' file.txt                # cols 1 & 3
awk -F',' '{print $2}' data.csv              # CSV col 2
awk '{sum += $1} END {print sum}' file.txt   # sum col 1
awk '$3 > 100 {print $0}' file.txt           # filter rows
recipes.notes: Default field separator is whitespace. `-F` sets it. `$0` is the whole line, `$1`/`$2`/... are fields. `NR` = line number.

recipes.title: grep: useful flags
recipes.code:
grep 'pattern' file.txt
grep -i 'pattern' file        # case-insensitive
grep -r 'pattern' dir/         # recursive
grep -l 'pattern' *.txt        # files with matches
grep -v 'pattern' file         # invert (lines NOT matching)
grep -n 'pattern' file         # line numbers
grep -E 'foo|bar' file         # extended regex (use -P for PCRE)
recipes.notes: `rg` (ripgrep) is way faster and respects gitignore — recommended for codebases. `-F` for literal string (no regex).

recipes.title: cut, sort, uniq, wc
recipes.code:
cut -d',' -f2,4 data.csv          # cols 2 & 4 from CSV
sort file.txt | uniq               # dedupe (sorted)
sort file.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn  # count occurrences
wc -l file.txt                     # line count
wc -w file.txt                      # word count
recipes.notes: `uniq` only dedupes ADJACENT lines — always pair with `sort` first. `sort -n` numeric, `sort -r` reverse.

recipes.title: jq: filter and transform JSON
recipes.code:
curl -s api/users | jq '.[] | .name'
jq '.users[] | select(.age > 30) | .name' users.json
jq -r '.users[].email' users.json     # raw (no quotes)
jq '{name: .name, total: (.items | length)}' user.json
recipes.notes: `.` is the identity filter. `.[]` iterates. `select()` filters. `-r` outputs raw strings (no JSON quotes) — useful in shell pipelines.

recipes.title: yq: process YAML
recipes.code:
yq '.database.host' config.yaml
yq '.users | length' config.yaml
yq -i '.version = "2.0"' config.yaml     # in-place edit
yq -o json config.yaml > config.json     # convert to JSON
recipes.notes: Two main yq tools: mikefarah/yq (Go, syntax like jq) and python-yq (Python wrapper around jq). They have different syntax — install mikefarah's via brew.

recipes.title: date: format and arithmetic
recipes.code:
date +%Y-%m-%d                       # 2026-05-14
date +%s                             # epoch
date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ           # UTC ISO

# GNU:
date -d '+7 days' +%Y-%m-%d
date -d '@1700000000'

# macOS/BSD:
date -v+7d +%Y-%m-%d
recipes.notes: GNU `date -d` and BSD `date -v` differ — write scripts for one or both. Install GNU date on macOS: `brew install coreutils` then use `gdate`.

recipes.title: Get absolute path
recipes.code:
realpath path/to/file
realpath --relative-to=/base path

# Portable (macOS lacks GNU realpath by default):
abs=$(cd "$(dirname "$1")" && pwd)/$(basename "$1")
recipes.notes: `realpath` is GNU; macOS may need `brew install coreutils` (then `grealpath`). The portable cd/dirname trick works almost anywhere.

recipes.title: Make a temp file or dir
recipes.code:
tmpfile=$(mktemp)
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmpfile" "$tmpdir"' EXIT

echo 'data' > "$tmpfile"
# ... use it ...
recipes.notes: Pair with a `trap ... EXIT` to clean up automatically. Use `-t prefix` to control the prefix name.

recipes.title: Get the script's own directory
recipes.code:
SCRIPT_DIR="$( cd "$( dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" )" && pwd )"
echo "script lives in: $SCRIPT_DIR"
recipes.notes: Use `BASH_SOURCE[0]` instead of `$0` so it works when sourced too. Doesn't resolve symlinks — wrap with `realpath` if you need that.

recipes.title: Compare numbers and strings
recipes.code:
# Numbers:
if (( a > b )); then echo big; fi
if [[ $a -gt $b ]]; then echo big; fi

# Strings:
if [[ "$s" == 'hello' ]]; then echo hi; fi
if [[ "$s" == hel* ]]; then echo prefix; fi
if [[ "$s" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then echo digits; fi
recipes.notes: Numeric: `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge` (or `(( ))`). String: `==` `!=` (with glob support in `[[ ]]`). `=~` for regex match.

recipes.title: Loop with index
recipes.code:
arr=(a b c d)
for i in "${!arr[@]}"; do
  echo "$i: ${arr[$i]}"
done
recipes.notes: `${!arr[@]}` gives the keys/indices. For C-style: `for ((i=0; i<${#arr[@]}; i++))`.

recipes.title: Glob patterns
recipes.code:
ls *.txt                   # any .txt
ls file?.txt               # one char
ls [abc]*                  # starts with a, b, or c

shopt -s globstar
ls **/*.py                 # recursive (bash 4+)

shopt -s nullglob          # empty pattern = nothing (not literal)
recipes.notes: Default behavior: an unmatched glob expands to the literal pattern (surprising). Set `nullglob` to make it expand to nothing instead.

recipes.title: Brace expansion
recipes.code:
echo {1..5}             # 1 2 3 4 5
echo {a..e}             # a b c d e
echo {01..10..2}        # 01 03 05 07 09
mv file.{txt,bak}        # mv file.txt file.bak
mkdir -p src/{js,css,img}
recipes.notes: Happens BEFORE variable/glob expansion. Useful for generating filenames, paths, sequences. Won't work inside double quotes.

recipes.title: Heredoc (multi-line strings)
recipes.code:
cat <<EOF
Hello $USER
today is $(date +%Y-%m-%d)
EOF

# No variable expansion:
cat <<'EOF'
$USER stays literal
EOF
recipes.notes: Quoted delimiter (`'EOF'`) disables expansion — useful for embedding scripts. `<<-EOF` strips leading TABS (not spaces).

recipes.title: Detect OS / distro
recipes.notes: `/etc/os-release` is the standard way to identify Linux distros. `uname -m` for architecture (x86_64, arm64).

recipes.title: curl POST JSON
recipes.code:
curl -fsSL -X POST 'https://api.example.com/items' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"banana"}'

# From a file:
curl -d @body.json -H 'Content-Type: application/json' URL
recipes.notes: `-f` fail on HTTP errors, `-s` silent, `-S` show errors anyway, `-L` follow redirects. Combine as `-fsSL` for scripts.

recipes.title: curl with retries
recipes.code:
curl --retry 5 --retry-delay 2 --retry-max-time 60 \
     --retry-connrefused \
     -fsSL URL
recipes.notes: `--retry-connrefused` (curl 7.52+) retries when the connection is refused — important for waiting on services starting up.

recipes.title: Wait for a port to open
recipes.code:
until nc -z localhost 5432; do
  echo 'waiting for postgres...'
  sleep 1
done
echo 'ready'
recipes.notes: `nc -z` does a zero-IO connect — pure port check. Alternative tools: `wait-for-it.sh`, `dockerize -wait`.

recipes.title: Watch a command
recipes.code:
watch -n 2 'ls -la'        # every 2 seconds
watch -d 'df -h'           # highlight differences
recipes.notes: Ships with most Linux distros; on macOS `brew install watch`. For one-shot loops, a `while sleep 2; do ...; done` works too.

recipes.title: Lock a file (flock)
recipes.notes: `flock -n` = non-blocking (exit if locked). Without `-n` it waits. Use FD 9 (arbitrary) to hold the lock for the subshell.

recipes.title: Run inside a tmux session
recipes.code:
tmux new -d -s mywork 'long-running-cmd'
tmux attach -t mywork
tmux ls
tmux kill-session -t mywork
recipes.notes: `-d` detached. Survives SSH disconnects. Alternative: `screen`. For modern setups, `tmux` is the default choice.

recipes.title: Schedule via cron
recipes.code:
# Edit:
crontab -e

# Examples:
0 9 * * *      /usr/local/bin/morning-job.sh
*/5 * * * *    /opt/scripts/heartbeat.sh
0 0 * * 0      /opt/scripts/weekly.sh

# Log output:
*/5 * * * *    cmd >> /var/log/cron.log 2>&1
recipes.notes: Cron runs with a minimal env — set PATH explicitly. Capture stderr or jobs fail silently. systemd timers are a modern alternative.

recipes.title: Send signals to processes
recipes.code:
kill 1234              # SIGTERM
kill -9 1234           # SIGKILL
kill -HUP 1234         # reload (common convention)

pkill nginx            # by name
pkill -f 'python app.py'  # match full cmdline
recipes.notes: SIGTERM (default) is polite — let the process clean up. SIGKILL (9) is forceful — no cleanup. Use `kill -l` to list signals.

recipes.title: Find process by name
recipes.code:
pgrep -f 'python app.py'
ps aux | grep '[p]ython app.py'    # the [p] trick avoids matching grep itself

# PID of last background job:
long-cmd & pid=$!
recipes.notes: `[p]ython` is a regex trick — `grep` won't match its own command line. `pgrep -f` matches full command (not just process name).

recipes.title: CPU / memory usage
recipes.code:
top -bn1 | head -20            # one snapshot
htop                            # interactive
free -h                         # memory
uptime                          # load avg
vmstat 1 5                      # 5 samples, 1s apart
recipes.notes: `top -bn1` is the scriptable form. macOS doesn't have `free` — use `vm_stat` or `top -l 1 | grep PhysMem`.

recipes.title: Disk usage by directory
recipes.code:
du -sh ./*           # one level
du -sh .             # total
du -h --max-depth=2 . | sort -h
df -h                # filesystem usage
recipes.notes: `-h` human-readable. `sort -h` understands human-readable sizes. On macOS BSD `du`, use `-d 2` instead of `--max-depth`.

recipes.title: tar gzip / extract
recipes.code:
# Create:
tar -czf archive.tar.gz dir/

# Extract:
tar -xzf archive.tar.gz
tar -xzf archive.tar.gz -C /target/dir

# List:
tar -tzf archive.tar.gz
recipes.notes: Flags: `c`reate, e`x`tract, `t`list, `z` gzip, `j` bzip2, `J` xz, `v` verbose, `f` file. Memorize `czf` and `xzf`.

recipes.title: Unzip a file
recipes.code:
unzip archive.zip
unzip archive.zip -d /target/dir
unzip -l archive.zip          # list contents

# Create:
zip -r archive.zip dir/
recipes.notes: `zip`/`unzip` may not be installed everywhere — `apt install unzip`. For tar archives, see the tar recipe.

recipes.title: Generate SSH key + push to server
recipes.code:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'me@example.com'
# accept default path ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

ssh-copy-id user@host
ssh user@host
recipes.notes: ed25519 is current best practice (faster + safer than RSA). Add to `~/.ssh/config` for an alias: `Host myserver\n  HostName ...\n  User ...`

recipes.title: rsync a directory
recipes.code:
# Local:
rsync -avh src/ dst/

# Remote:
rsync -avh --progress src/ user@host:/path/

# Mirror (delete extras at dest):
rsync -avh --delete src/ dst/
recipes.notes: Trailing `/` on `src/` matters — `src/` copies contents, `src` copies the dir itself. `-a` archive (preserves perms, times, etc.). `--dry-run` to preview.

recipes.title: Watch a directory for changes
recipes.code:
# Linux (apt install inotify-tools):
inotifywait -mr -e modify,create,delete src/ | while read path event file; do
  echo "$event $path$file"
done

# macOS (brew install fswatch):
fswatch -r src/ | while read change; do echo "$change"; done
recipes.notes: For dev hot-reload, tools like `entr`, `nodemon`, `watchexec` are friendlier wrappers. `watchexec -r cmd` reruns on any change.

recipes.title: Print colored output
recipes.code:
RED='\033[31m'
GREEN='\033[32m'
BOLD='\033[1m'
RESET='\033[0m'

printf "${RED}error:${RESET} %s\n" 'something failed'
printf "${GREEN}${BOLD}ok${RESET}\n"
recipes.notes: Use `printf` (not `echo -e`) for portability. Check `[[ -t 1 ]]` and skip colors when stdout isn't a TTY (e.g. logs to file).

recipes.title: Parse flags with getopts
recipes.notes: `v` = flag, `n:` = takes an arg. Only handles short options. For long options use `getopt` (note: not portable across BSD/GNU).

recipes.title: Source another script
recipes.code:
source ./common.sh
. ./common.sh           # same thing, POSIX

# Guard against being executed:
# (in common.sh)
if [[ "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" == "${0}" ]]; then
  echo 'this file is meant to be sourced'
  exit 1
fi
recipes.notes: Sourcing runs the file in the current shell — definitions persist. Executing runs it in a subshell — changes don't escape.

recipes.title: Clone a repo
recipes.code:
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
git clone git@github.com:user/repo.git target-dir

# Shallow (faster, no full history):
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/user/repo.git

# Specific branch:
git clone -b dev --single-branch URL
recipes.notes: `--depth 1` saves time/space for huge repos but limits some operations (like git log). Use SSH URL if you have a key set up.

recipes.title: Init a new repo
recipes.code:
git init
git init -b main           # set initial branch name

# With first commit:
git init && echo '# project' > README.md && git add . && git commit -m 'init'
recipes.notes: Configure default branch globally: `git config --global init.defaultBranch main`.

recipes.title: Stage files
recipes.code:
git add file.txt
git add .                       # current dir + subdirs
git add -A                      # all changes in repo
git add -p                      # interactively pick hunks
git add -u                      # only update tracked files (no new)
recipes.notes: `-p` is great for crafting focused commits. `git add .` only adds within cwd; `git add -A` is repo-wide.

recipes.title: Unstage files
recipes.code:
git restore --staged file.txt
git restore --staged .          # everything

# Older syntax (still works):
git reset HEAD file.txt
